title: The SHOCKING Reality of Being an Astronaut
description:
SSpace travel, while often romanticized, presents numerous challenges and dangers that astronauts must face. This video explores the stark realities of space exploration, detailing issues from zero gravity and body changes to real-life incidents during NASA missions. As NASA completes the Artemis 2 moon mission, understanding astronaut survival and the risks of cosmic radiation and space accidents becomes crucial for future human endeavors beyond Earth.

From the early struggles of astronauts like Alan Shepard to modern missions like the Artemis II mission, space exploration continues to push human limits. Even today, astronauts aboard spacecraft and space stations deal with issues like toilet malfunctions, isolation, radiation exposure, and life-threatening emergencies.

We also examine real incidents like the Skylab 4 crisis, spacewalk dangers, and how astronauts survive in extreme conditions far beyond Earth. As NASA prepares for the Artemis II moon mission and future human space exploration, understanding these challenges becomes more important than ever.

If you’ve searched for astronaut problems, Artemis II mission, NASA moon mission, life in space, or what happens to the human body in space, this video gives you the rational perspective. Don’t forget to subscribe, like, comment, and share…

transcript: We look at astronauts floating in space and see beauty, silence, and calm. A true victory for science and humanity, but that image hides a reality that is far more complex, far more dangerous, far more unforgiving than we usually imagine. In space, nothing works the way you think it does, not even something as simple as going to the bathroom. Space travel is something that only a few hundred people in the history of humanity have ever experienced. And astronauts are often seen as figures of admiration, especially by children. Today, with missions like Artemis capturing global attention, most of what we hear is about achievements, images, and milestones. But in all this excitement, there is something we tend to ignore. When we look at astronauts as heroes, as people belonging to an elite and adventurous profession, there are certain realities that we do not pay attention to. Although the profession appears glamorous and heroic, the life of an astronaut is far more complex and far more challenging than we usually imagine. And what we rarely see is what their life actually feels like. Hello, I'm Anand and you're watching Pale Blue Thoughts, a channel where we explore science, rational thinking, and the reality behind the stories we often take for granted. If you enjoy this kind of content, consider subscribing and sharing it with others. Come, let's explore the world of astronauts today. Let us begin with a real incident. Let's talk about the experience of Alan Shepard, the first American [music] astronaut. For this mission, he was dressed in a space suit, secured inside a spacecraft, connected to multiple sensors, loaded into a rocket, and prepared for launch. It was supposed to be a short flight of about 15 minutes. And this was only a few months after Yuri Gagarin had made the first human space flight in 1961. However, the launch did not happen as planned. One technical issue after another kept appearing, and the launch was repeatedly delayed, forcing Shepard to remain inside the spacecraft, fully suited and strapped in. Not for 15 minutes, but for nearly 5 to 6 hours. During the time, something very basic happened. He needed to urinate. >> [music] >> On Earth, this is not even something we think about, but in that situation, it became a serious problem because once an astronaut is suited up and secured inside a spacecraft, removing him is not simple. The suit is sealed, sensors are attached, and the entire system [music] is built around that configuration. So, detaching everything could create even more delays and complications. Ground control asked him to hold it, and he tried, but the delays continued. Eventually, Shepard made it clear that he could not hold it anymore, and there was only one option left. He turned off the sensors and urinated inside the space suit. There was concern that the liquid could damage the equipment, but his undergarments absorbed it, and the suit's [music] internal systems managed the situation well enough for the mission to proceed. That moment taught engineers [music] an important lesson. No matter how advanced the mission is, it must account for the most basic human needs. Even today, during the preparation of missions like Artemis, [music] this lesson still applies. During testing and simulation of modern spacecraft systems, engineers have encountered similar problems in waste management systems, including airflow failures and even freezing of moisture inside the system. These are not dramatic failures, and that is exactly the point because in space, even small problems do not stay [music] small. What appears to be a minor inconvenience on Earth can become a serious risk in space. And these are issues we are discovering even before humans begin long-duration missions beyond [music] Earth. Now, let us move from that incident to everyday life in space. Today, we permanently inhabit structures like the International Space Station, which orbits the Earth at an altitude of about 400 km and houses astronauts for months at a time. It is a massive structure, roughly the size of a football stadium, but life inside it is fundamentally different from life on Earth, starting from the most basic routines. Consider something as simple as waking up in the morning. On Earth, our sense of time is structured by sunrise and sunset, but in space, the station completes one orbit around the Earth approximately every 90 minutes, which means astronauts experience around 16 sunrises and sunsets in a single day. This completely disrupts the idea of a normal day and has direct impact on the biological clock. Now, think about the next step in a typical morning routine, which is going to the washroom. On Earth, gravity takes care of everything, but in space, there is very less gravity, and as a result, nothing moves downward and everything floats. This happens because the space station is in continuous free fall around the Earth. It is moving forward at such a high speed that although it is constantly falling towards the Earth, it keeps missing it, and this creates the condition known as microgravity. In such an environment, there is no natural direction of up [music] or down, and because of that, urine does not fall, and neither does any other form of waste. Instead, astronauts must rely on suction-based systems, but using these systems is not simple as it sounds. They must carefully align their bodies and often strap themselves into position because otherwise, they would simply float away. Even a slight misalignment can cause a system to fail, and if that happens, the waste does not fall into the ground, but instead [music] floats inside the spacecraft. In a closed environment filled with sensitive equipment, this is not just unpleasant, but potentially dangerous. Now, let us talk about hygiene, which is another area where life in space becomes very different from what we are used to on Earth. Water is an extremely limited resource in space, and almost everything is recycled, including urine, which is purified and reused as drinking water. Because of this limitation, bathing in the way we do on Earth is not possible. The problem is not just the availability of water, but also the behavior of water itself because in the absence of gravity, water does not flow downward, but instead forms floating droplets that sticks to surfaces or drift through the spacecraft. [music] This makes even simple activities like washing or cleaning much more complicated. The same applies to brushing teeth because if water escapes, it does not fall, but floats, and if a toothbrush slips, it does not drop, but drifts away. Because of this, astronauts must handle even the smallest objects with precision, ensuring that everything is controlled and secured at all times. Sleeping is also affected by this environment. On Earth, we lie down because gravity holds us in place, but in space, the body floats, so astronauts sleep inside sleeping bags that are attached to the walls of the spacecraft. In some cases, they even secure their hands so that their limbs do not drift while they are asleep. Moreover, sleep in space is also carefully scheduled because every activity is planned in advance, and astronauts must follow a strict routine to maintain both physical and mental stability. Even sweating behaves differently. On Earth, sweat drips down due to gravity, but in space, it remains on the skin, forming a layer that must be wiped away manually, making even basic hygiene a continuous effort. Food presents another set of challenges. Small crumbs can float into sensitive equipment and damage systems, and at the same time, fluid shifts in the body cause more fluid to move towards the head, making the face appear puffy and reducing the sense of smell, which in turn affects taste and makes food seem bland. But all of this is still only part of the problem. Now, let us consider the impact on the human body. You may have seen astronauts exercising inside spacecraft and wondered [music] why it is necessary even during short missions. The reason is that without gravity, the human body begins to weaken much faster than we expect. In microgravity, muscles weaken because they are no longer required to support body weight, [music] and bones gradually lose density over time. Astronauts can even grow slightly taller because the spine expands in the absence of gravity. But these changes come at a cost, and without regular exercise, the body [music] deteriorates quickly. For this reason, astronauts must exercise for at least 2 hours every day to maintain their physical condition. Even something as simple as an itch becomes a problem because there is no easy way to scratch inside the suit, and astronauts have even improvised solutions like attaching small Velcro patches inside their helmets to deal with this. Beyond these physical changes, there are serious safety concerns because in space, even a small problem does not remain small. A minor leak, a small fire, or even a loose object can escalate into a life-threatening situation, and unlike on Earth, there is no easy way to escape. If something goes wrong, the crew is confined within the spacecraft. Now, consider missions like Artemis, which go beyond low Earth orbit and take astronauts into deep space. Unlike the International Space Station, which remains relatively close to Earth, these missions involve traveling much farther away inside spacecrafts like Orion, where space is limited and immediate rescue is not possible. This distance increases isolation, increases dependence on onboard systems, and significantly increases the consequences of even smallest failure. In addition, astronauts are exposed to higher levels of cosmic radiation, which adds [music] another layer of risk. Apart from physical challenges, there are also psychological challenges. Astronauts live in confined spaces with very little privacy, with almost no personal space, often with the same group of people for extended periods. This can become mentally exhausting over time. For example, if conflicts arise, there is no way to distance oneself. Also, being so far away from family adds to the sense of isolation. Even emotional experiences are affected. When astronauts cry, tears do not fall, but instead accumulate around the eyes, making even the simple human response uncomfortable. This kind of psychological strain is not just theoretical. During the Skylab mission in the 1970s, astronauts experienced significant fatigue and stress due to an extremely demanding schedule. At one point, communication with mission control was briefly disrupted, not as a rebellion, but as a result of exhaustion and misjudgment. [music] The situation was later resolved, and it led to an important realization that even highly trained astronauts are still human, and their limits must be respected. This experience pushed NASA to better understand the psychological demands of long-duration missions, including [music] the importance of rest, balance, and sustainable workloads. It is also important to remember that astronauts are constantly working. They conduct scientific experiments, perform maintenance, and repair systems, and every task must be done with precision because even a small mistake can have serious consequences. A floating tool or a misplaced object can damage critical equipment. Spacewalks are among the most demanding and dangerous activities. Astronauts must operate outside the spacecraft [music] in bulky, pressurized suits for several hours, and these suits function as complete life support systems. Even a minor malfunction can become dangerous, and there have been instances where water leaked into an astronaut's helmet, creating [music] a life-threatening situation. Apart from all this, astronauts also handle routine maintenance, cleaning, and repairs because there is no separate support staff, no counter by to look after their needs, and any failure in these tasks can affect the entire mission. At every moment, there is an underlying awareness that something could go wrong, and that creates a continuous psychological pressure that astronauts must learn to live with. When they return to Earth after months in space, their bodies must readjust to gravity. Muscles are weakened, coordination is affected, and even simple actions like standing or walking can feel difficult at first, requiring [music] time and rehabilitation. So, even though space travel appears glamorous from the outside, the reality is very different. The life of an astronaut is not just about intelligence or achievement, but about surviving in an environment that is fundamentally hostile to human life. When we see an astronaut floating in space, yes, we see beauty, calmness, and silence, but behind that image lies constant effort, control, [music] and survival. There is no air, no natural pressure, and nothing in that environment that supports life. So, everything that keeps them alive is [music] artificial and fragile. As we move further into deep space, this reality becomes even more extreme and more unforgiving. These are the [music] same challenges that future astronauts will face as we attempt to build long-term human presence on the moon and eventually on Mars, where survival will depend entirely on technology and precision. And yet, we keep planning to go out there, not because it is easy or safe, but because pushing beyond our limits is what defines us as a species. In that environment, there is no second chance because space does not forgive mistakes. >> [music]
